1:
Keil and Delitzsch place the oracle structurally. This second type of heathen pride closes the series against the nations as Babylon opened it: Babylon the city of the world's imperial power, Tyre of its commerce, the one the centre of the greatest land power, the other of the greatest maritime power. The first subjugated the nations with an iron arm and secured its rule by deportation; the second took their treasures as peaceably as it could and secured its advantage by colonies and factories. He adds that the Phoenician cities formed at first six or eight independent states under kings, Sidon much older and alone named by the law and by Homer, Tyre rising into notoriety only after David's time though by the Assyrian era holding a kind of supremacy.

The date and destroyer are argued. Adam Clarke has the prophecy denounce Tyre's destruction by Nebuchadnezzar a hundred and twenty years before the event, when the Tyrians were prosperous and the Babylonians in abject subjection to Assyria, so that such an outcome was improbable in the highest degree; the seventy years he makes the days of one kingdom, the duration of the Babylonian empire, since otherwise the prophecy cannot fit. John Calvin reports the rival view, that the reference is to Alexander's storming of Tyre, which he took with great difficulty. John Wesley takes both, since Tyre was destroyed first by the one and afterwards by the other, the prophecy respecting the former directly and the latter also.

Charles Ellicott reconstructs the politics instead. The chapter, he says, calls us to enquire into Tyre's relations at the time, learned partly from Scripture and partly from Assyrian inscriptions. In the days of David and Solomon there had been an intimate alliance between Israel and Tyre's king, one psalm indicating an interchange of kingly gifts if not tribute, another, which he connects with a later reign, showing the alliance passed into hostility. Tyre's position threw it into closer relations with the northern kingdom, its country nourished by the king's country, and he thinks the pretender Pekah and Rezin meant to set on Judah's throne was a Tyrian ruler's son.

The howling and the silence are one gesture. Matthew Henry observes that the prophecy fitly begins and ends with the ships, all the city's business and honour depending on its shipping, and Tyre is shown flourishing so her fall may appear the more dismal; the merchants of the older city first replenished her, the daughter outgrowing the mother, a mortification to great cities. Clarke makes silence a mark of grief and quotes the elders of Zion sitting on the ground with dust on their heads. Ellicott calls the dumbness that of stupefied terror, and would render isle as coast, fitting the narrow seaboard strip the Phoenicians held. Calvin gives the reason: they are silent because they will make no more voyages to Tyre, stunned like men who dare not open their mouth. John Gill notes Tyre stood off the shore, an island until Alexander joined it to the mainland.

The third verse is Egyptian. Gill identifies Sihor as the Nile, named from the blackness of its waters, the seed being what grew on its banks or by its overflow, corn and flax and paper. Clarke adds the ancient names given for the same reason and a Latin line on the black sand that makes green Egypt fertile, supplying the neighbouring nations with corn. Ellicott completes the trade: Egyptian corn was a chief branch of Tyrian commerce, and since the Egyptians had no timber and mostly hated the sea, their navy consisted of Phoenicians, so Tyre practically reaped the harvest of the Nile's inundation. Calvin says the wealth is extolled so God's judgment may be the more manifest, the calamity the more evidently his work for being unexpected. Delitzsch marks the turn from coast-land to ancestral city.
4:
Zidon is shamed as the mother. Gill sets her twenty-five miles off, so allied in trade that her daughter's fall must confound her and make her fear the same next. Clarke cites Justin: the Sidonians, driven out by Ascalon's king, took ship and built beside Tyre. Ellicott makes the strength of the sea the rock-island of the newer town, and sees Zidon a widow bereaved, powerless to crowd her streets again. Calvin hears a taunt put into Tyre's own mouth, jesting at her boast of colonies: Pliny named Utica, Cadiz beyond the world's limits, and Carthage that aspired to govern it, though her whole superiority now consists of scarlet and purple. Wesley calls Tyre the sea's strength for guarding that water from piracy, and hears a fruitful woman confess barrenness.

The report reaches Egypt, and the survivors run west. Gill recalls how news of the plagues and the drowning once panicked the neighbouring nations. Ellicott would translate when the report cometh to Egypt, whose dismay is practical: her corn export ran through Tyre, an outpost besides against Assyrian kings pressing on the Ethiopian dynasty. Calvin takes the joint ruin as proof that an earlier devastation is meant, not Alexander's day when Tyre was a free state; Egypt is punished for prompting the Jews to rebel under pretence of friendship. Delitzsch measures the flight by distance: not Cyprus, not Carthage, but Tartessus, farthest and hardest to reach. Gill canvasses Spain, Cilicia, the Targum's province of the sea and the Septuagint's Carthage, with Kimchi addressing the summons to traders rather than citizens. Ellicott hears irony: they go to the far end of their commerce, not for wealth now but asylum.

Her antiquity is turned against her. Gill sees a city gay and brisk only the other day. Clarke insists Tyre was already fortified in Joshua's day, and reads her own feet carrying her as the inhabitants shifting the town from mainland to island; the new site lay half a mile off, but the word for far denotes interval, not great space, as when it measures camp from ark. Ellicott, following Josephus, dates the foundation two hundred and forty years before Solomon, preferring the sense her feet are wont to carry her, which points at the colonies. Calvin makes the antiquity a boast and banishment its answer: exile with poverty is extreme, and these lack even a beast to carry them. Wesley pictures a delicate lady never setting foot to the ground, borne about in chariots.

Then the question that names the author. Gill wonders who could conceive the scheme against the queen of cities, still less accomplish it, and concludes no mortal was concerned. Ellicott presses the participle: crowning is transitive, Tyre the distributor of crowns to her colonies; the word for merchant, he notes, is the word for Canaanite. Calvin refuses to read the verse as bare astonishment and binds it to the answer following, the question rousing sluggish hearers who would else despise the judgment. He turns contemporary without warning: Venice merchants reckoning themselves equals of princes, Antwerp factors outspending the nobility. Wesley answers flatly that this is the word of God and not of man.

The answer is purpose, and its object is pride. Gill names a counsellor wonderful in counsel and able to execute it. Ellicott hears the verb's first sense, to pollute, perhaps glancing at Melkarth's temple, reckoned among the oldest anywhere. Calvin makes it a lesson in providence: we may never divide God's wisdom and justice from his power, and the schoolmen's absolute power is blasphemy, a tyrant acting by caprice, like the heathen fancy of a god sporting with human affairs. Scripture states its reasons: here, the vices that follow abundance in trading towns. Rank is not itself hateful to God, only the contempt that clings to it. Wesley reads the design as the abasing of every potentate on earth.
10:
Nobody agrees who the daughter of Tarshish is. Gill, with the Vulgate, makes her Tyre, the sea's own child, and hears the citizens told to run out as swiftly as a river; Kimchi would send them to Tarshish itself, but the accent on river forbids it, so Gill prefers the traders of Tarshish hurrying home before the ruin. Wesley agrees she is Tyre, born of the sea and nursed by it. Ellicott reads the opposite: Tarshish herself is meant, spreading like the Nile in flood because the colony is subject no longer, with no tribute and no limit on her trade. Clarke, following Lowth, takes the girdle for a dam, the burst city a river with its banks down and its waters wasted; Calvin prefers ditches, mounds and ramparts, since the poorest merchants sell girdles.

The hand goes out over the water. Gill remembers another sea and Pharaoh. Delitzsch will not shrink the shaken kingdoms to the small Phoenician states: God reaching across the sea threw western Asia and Egypt into anxious excitement and summoned them as instruments against Kena'an; Phoenicia called itself Canaan, and this is the only place in the older Scriptures where the name narrows so far. Ellicott counts the convulsion wider still, Babylon and Syria and Judah shaken as Assyria revived under Tiglath-pileser; merchant city, he notes, is literally Canaan, the noun for city an interpolation. Calvin declines the older reading of past deliverances; Tyre cannot perish alone, and no siege-engine is wanted where the bare will of God suffices. Wesley makes the commandment the courage put into her enemies.

The virgin is told she will not sing. Gill limits the silence to seventy years, after which the harp returns. Ellicott finds the phrase self-contradictory, the adjective meaning defiled: Tyre had never lost a battle, her citadel virgin until now. He hears irony again in the flight to Cyprus, which the Assyrian kings boast of taxing in their inscriptions as the land in the sea of the setting sun. Calvin denies any praise of chastity; the point is that treasures kept in faithful custody are about to be violated, as one might say Venice keeps her virginity because no force has taken her. Chittim, he adds, reaches past Cilicia to Greece and Italy: no rest among neighbours, none among strangers. Wesley says she had never worn a conqueror's yoke.

Then the chapter's strangest verse. Clarke calls it extremely obscure, agents and pronouns shifting number and gender, the manuscripts no help and the versions little; he reads ethnology, tracing the Chaldeans to Abraham's kindred, a rude wandering people of no account, addicted to rapine like wild Arabians, until an Assyrian king gathered them into Babylon. Calvin agrees, adding that they lived under skins before Assyria civilised them, and that the verb means to build, not destroy; the daughter afterwards devoured the mother, so what could Tyre expect from both? Wesley puts Nimrod at the founding. Ellicott rejects the approach: the towers are Assyrian siege-works, the palaces Babylon's under Sargon and Sennacherib, and a scrap of doubtful ethnology does not cohere with the context.

The howl returns and closes the frame. Ellicott marks the repetition, the woe ending where it began, and identifies the wasted strength as the fortress. Wesley makes it the city where the traders found safety and wealth. Calvin has the Cilicians, near neighbours and constant customers, amazed at a shut harbour, their strength because no other route made a voyage pay. Clarke sets beside it a later prophet's lament: the princes of the sea coming down from their thrones, laying aside their robes, clothed with trembling and seated on the ground. Delitzsch is already past the ruin: the days of one king are a fixed span, an eastern reckoning where one sovereign will settles everything, and seventy is ten sevens, a stereotyped figure for such a period.
15:
Everyone counts the seventy years differently. Clarke makes them one kingdom's span, from Nebuchadnezzar's first conquests to Cyrus taking Babylon, with Tyre falling near the middle, so she served barely half the term though released with the rest at its close. Wesley narrows the king to Nebuchadnezzar's race, ending in his son's son. Henry keeps the dynasty and adds the release, presuming Cyrus sent the Tyrians home with the Jews. Ellicott finds no Assyrian or Babylonian reign of such length and reads the phrase as days a king appoints, an absolute decree. Calvin takes it for the ordinary age of a man, seventy by the Psalmist's reckoning, a king being named because Tyre dated her years by her king's life, which puts the prediction beyond human conjecture.

The song is a trade song. Ellicott hears a tone divided between irony and pity, and recalls that the East's singing women were commonly of this class; the old lovers summoned are old allies. Calvin draws the picture: an aged harlot, unable to forget her gains, walking the city with harp and voice, seized with the madness such women feel when age has made them invisible, as Horace mocked Lydia; the sweet melody is the merchant's flattery driving men into his net. Delitzsch grounds the word for prostitution in the trade itself, which acknowledges no limit God has set and makes itself common to all: a prostitution of the soul. Clarke adds a traveller's note: the old women sing while the young ones dance.

Then the visitation. Henry insists the visitor is not her old acquaintance, the colonies she planted having forgotten her, but the Lord by some unthought-of turn. Ellicott sets the revival under the Persian kings. Clarke follows the city down the centuries: recovered after Nebuchadnezzar and again after Alexander, Christian early and holding fourteen bishoprics, lost to the Saracens, retaken, lost to the Mamelukes and then the Turks, sunk at last to a bare rock, a place to spread nets upon. Calvin makes the mercy a doctrine, God never being so harsh as to withhold mitigation, then turns it against her: she is no better for the chastisement, and returns to a trade so full of contrivances for gain that only a man long trained in it can follow them. Wesley notes her hire is properly a harlot's fee.

The reversal startles the commentators. Ellicott points out that the law forbade gifts of that origin at the sanctuary, yet the penitent harlot city may bring them in; read religiously the verse admits proselytes, read politically it restores the old alliance of Solomon's day. Gill and Wesley take it as the Tyrians' conversion in the earliest Christian centuries, Gill adding that Jewish commentators refer it to the Messiah's days. Delitzsch is careful: not conversion but something approaching it, the profane trade made to serve a holy purpose, its profit no longer capitalised. Calvin marvels that goodness reached this brothel and almost hell, and dismisses the worry whether cheating money may be offered to God: the prophet describes her after repentance, not during her fornication.

The last clause disposes of the money. Henry gives it to the priests attending the temple, not in pomp but that they may eat sufficiently and wear durable clothing, plain and grave as an old man's; he wonders whether captivity beside the Jews, who had prophets with them, first turned the Tyrians from idols. Ellicott reads those who dwell before the Lord as citizens of Jerusalem, supplied from Tyre with food and raiment, and recalls Tyrians helping to build the second temple as they built the first. Calvin allows the priests but stops nowhere short: since all believers are a royal priesthood, the household of faith has first claim; and he presses cheerfulness, since men reckon whatever they give away as lost. Wesley forbids the hoarding that covetousness once required.
